name: Ivan Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Ivan. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential. What's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm farm manager on the Ashworth estate, so I don't own the land, I run it for the family that does. It's 900 hectares, mostly wheat, barley and beans, with 1,200 ewes on the hill ground. I've six staff. A typical day is a quick meeting in the yard at seven, then I'm in the pickup checking crops, ringing the grain merchant, sorting out whoever's off sick.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How much does technology figure in that?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: More every year. The sprayer and the drill run on GPS, and we've yield maps from the combine. I'll use an AI chat tool now and then to sum up a long report or check a regulation, but I don't trust it with anything that matters. I'm never the first to try something, but I'm never the last either, and that's served me well for twenty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. Most of what was promised never matched what happens in a muddy field. At the grain merchant's open day, I'd say we got a few handy tools and that's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it'd be a relief for my job. My boss, old Mr Ashworth, likes having a manager he can phone. Nothing would push him to change that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going as I am. I'd use the AI tools a bit more for paperwork, the subsidy forms especially. I'd keep pushing the estate to replace the old combine, which needs doing anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Business as usual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone on the team who'd see it differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kasia, our sprayer operator, would be a bit disappointed, she reads all about the drones. The others wouldn't notice. Two of them have been on the estate longer than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about your household?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My wife Clara works in an insurance office in town, and I think she'd be more relieved than me. Clara's job is the one I thought AI would come for first, not mine, so a fizzle suits us both.

S0.say: I'd say I'm not surprised, because most promises don't survive a muddy field. At the grain merchant's open day I'd say we got a few handy tools and that's fine.
S0.think: Privately it'd be a relief for my job, since the estate owner likes having a manager he can phone. Nothing would push him to change that.
S0.do: Keeps going as he is and uses AI tools a bit more for subsidy forms and paperwork. Keeps pushing the estate to replace the old combine.
S0.quote: Clara's job is the one I thought AI would come for first, not mine, so a fizzle suits us both.
S0.fieldNote: Ivan is an employee, not an owner, and his security depends on his boss's habits. He's measured and middle-of-the-road. He immediately thinks of his wife's office job as the more exposed one, which shapes the household's view.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a change we need to manage, not fight. Use what works, drop what doesn't. I'd say that to the estate and to the lads in the yard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the estate would cut staff. Six people on 900 hectares is already lean, and with robot sprayers and self-driving tractors they'd want four. I'd probably keep my job, because someone has to run it, but I'd be the one choosing who goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait to see what the neighbouring estates buy and how it goes, maybe six months. Then I'd put a plan to the Ashworths: one robot sprayer, and Kasia trained to run it. I'd learn the farm management software properly myself, over a winter. And I'd push for anyone who leaves to get decent notice and a reference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Mostly about the staff conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you be most worried about losing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Big Tom, honestly. He's 61, he's brilliant with sheep and useless with screens. Choosing between Tom and a robot sprayer is a sum the estate would do in a minute, and I'd hate every number in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Clara's job be affected?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, insurance claims are exactly the sort of thing AI would do. She'd be changing how she works more than me. We'd be fine with the savings, but we'd both be adjusting.

S1.say: I'd say this is a change to manage, not fight, by using what works and dropping what doesn't. I'd say that to the estate and to the staff in the yard.
S1.think: Privately I think the estate would cut from six staff to four once robot sprayers and self-driving tractors arrived. I'd probably keep my job but would be the one choosing who goes.
S1.do: Watches what neighbouring estates buy for about six months, then proposes one robot sprayer with Kasia trained to run it. Learns the farm management software properly over winter and pushes for fair notice and references for anyone who leaves.
S1.feel: Uneasy, mostly about having the staff conversation.
S1.quote: Choosing between Tom and a robot sprayer is a sum the estate would do in a minute, and I'd hate every number in it.
S1.fieldNote: Ivan's role puts him between the owners and the staff, and that's where his discomfort sits. He's methodical: wait six months, then propose something small. He expects his wife's office job to change more than his, which keeps the household view balanced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and somebody should have seen it coming. I wouldn't be on a soapbox, but I'd say the government needs to pay people while they find their feet. I'd say it to anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the manager's job goes, along with most of the team. If a robot can plan the crops and run the machines, the Ashworths need a contractor and a laptop, not me. And it'd hit Clara's office at the same time, which is the bit that scares me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop any big spending at home that week, no kitchen, no new car. I'd move as much as possible into paying down the mortgage. I'd also lean on family: my brother has a building firm, and building might hold up longer than farming. And honestly I'd start looking at jobs that need a person in the room, though I don't know which ones those are any more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Two incomes going at once is what keeps me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said plenty of farm jobs nearby. Does that help here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not if every estate does the same thing in the same year. There are plenty of farm manager jobs nearby right up until there aren't any, and in two years that's how it would go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Leo and Nina?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leo's fourteen, he'd understand. I'd tell him we've got savings and a plan, and I'd try to sound like I meant it. Nina would just ask if we'd still have the dog.

S2.say: I'd say it's too fast and someone should have seen it coming. I'd say, without getting on a soapbox, that the government needs to pay people while they find their feet.
S2.think: Privately I think the manager's job and most of the team would go, because the estate would need a contractor and a laptop instead. It would hit Clara's office job at the same time, which scares me most.
S2.do: Halts big household spending that week, including the kitchen and a new car, and moves money into paying down the mortgage. Leans on his brother's building firm as a possible fallback and starts looking for work that needs a person on site.
S2.feel: Alarmed, kept awake by the thought of two incomes going at once.
S2.quote: There are plenty of farm manager jobs nearby right up until there aren't any, and in two years that's how it would go.
S2.fieldNote: Ivan's alarm comes from losing both household incomes at once, since he and Clara are both employees. He quickly dismisses the comfort of nearby jobs because every estate would change in the same year. He leans on family rather than politics, which fits his middle-of-the-road views.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, so let's use it. I'd tell the estate I want to be the one who runs the changeover, and I'd say to the team to get trained now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years gives me a chance. If I'm the person who knows how to run a robot estate, I'm worth keeping, at least for a while. Clara would have time to retrain too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do a proper course on farm robotics and data, the one the agricultural college runs at weekends. I'd push the Ashworths to trial one robot by year two, so we learn before everyone else. I'd keep saving and overpaying the mortgage, and I'd talk to Clara about what she'd retrain into.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's the kind of anxious that gets you up early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: That's quite a jump from 'never first' to trialling robots by year two. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the timetable's changed, not me. I still wouldn't buy the first robot on the market. I'd let a neighbour buy the first one, and I'd make sure we bought the second one before anyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them straight, at the yard meeting, and offer to pay for the course for anyone who wants it. Kasia would go for it. Big Tom would retire, I think, and I'd help him time it right.

S3.say: I'd say five years is fair warning and we should use it. I'd tell the estate I want to run the changeover and urge the team to get trained now.
S3.think: Privately five years gives me a chance, because a manager who can run a robot estate is worth keeping for a while. Clara would have time to retrain too.
S3.do: Takes the agricultural college's weekend course in farm robotics and data in the first year and pushes the estate to trial one robot by year two. Keeps overpaying the mortgage and plans Clara's retraining with her.
S3.feel: Anxious, but in a way that gets him up early.
S3.quote: I'd let a neighbour buy the first one, and I'd make sure we bought the second one before anyone else.
S3.fieldNote: Ivan explains his faster move as the timetable changing, not his nature. He'd still let a neighbour go first but wants to be second. He offers his team paid training and plans Big Tom's retirement with care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and anyone who doesn't plan has only themselves to blame. Maybe that's harsh. I'd say it more kindly at the yard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be fine. I'd be 53, the mortgage nearly done, and I'd have years to learn the new kit. I'd worry more about Leo, who'd be 24.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on for a few years and watch. Around year three or four, I'd do the robotics course and push the estate to trial kit. I'd help Clara retrain at her own pace. And I'd talk to Leo about university, steering him towards something hands-on and hard to replace, if there is such a thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in the background.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said anyone who doesn't plan has only themselves to blame. Do you believe that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half of it. Some people can't plan, they're living week to week. It's easy to say plan ahead when you've got a year's wages in the bank, and I know that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you hope Leo does?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hope he does something he loves. If he wanted to farm, I'd say learn the robots and the soil both. I don't know what else to tell him.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty of time and people who don't plan have mostly themselves to blame. I'd say it more kindly in the yard.
S4.think: Privately I'd be fine at 53 with the mortgage nearly done and years to learn the new kit. I'd worry more about my son Leo, who'd be 24.
S4.do: Carries on and watches for a few years, then takes the robotics course and pushes the estate to trial kit around year three or four. Helps Clara retrain at her own pace and talks to Leo about a hands-on university course.
S4.quote: It's easy to say plan ahead when you've got a year's wages in the bank, and I know that.
S4.fieldNote: Ivan goes back to his natural rhythm with ten years: watch, then follow. When challenged he softens his line about people who don't plan and admits his savings make it easy to say. His worry shifts to his son's future.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because Clara and I would both be hit at the same time. What would help is pay for people while they retrain, a year or so, and the estates being made to give staff proper notice and training before they bring the robots in.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the owners. People like the Ashworths would come out of this richer. I'm not angry about it, it's their land, but somebody should be asking what they owe the people who worked it.

headlineQuote: I'm never the first to try something, but I'm never the last either, and that's served me well for twenty years.
portrait: Ivan Fischer is 43 and manages the 900-hectare Ashworth estate, arable land plus 1,200 ewes, for the family who own it, with a team of six. He's a careful follower who uses AI tools now and then and prides himself on being neither first nor last. As an employee married to an insurance office worker, he's most shaken by fast AGI because both household incomes would go at once. With more time he plans to retrain and lead the estate's changeover, while worrying about his long-serving staff and his son.
biggestWorry: AGI in two years, because he and his wife would lose their incomes at the same time.
whatWouldHelp: Pay for people while they retrain for about a year, and rules making estates give staff notice and training before bringing in robots.
